Period schedule:

Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: First Meeting with the Farmer and the King

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (pp.78–81): story read-aloud with prediction prompt.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly introduces the chapter title 'Thank God!' and asks students what they think the story might be about, inviting a quick sharing of ideas. This opens up curiosity about the farmer and the king.
Teacher reads the story aloud from the textbook (pp.78–81), using varied expression for the farmer, his wife, and the king. Students follow along in their books.

Let us read — prediction prompt (p.79): Teacher pauses at the prediction moment and invites students to share what they think will happen next. Two or three students respond orally before the reading continues.
Teacher reads the remainder of the story aloud to its conclusion, then invites a short whole-class retelling — who was in the story, what happened, what the farmer said at the end.

periods.teacher_notes: The story's humour lies in the farmer's clever reframing of an embarrassing situation into gratitude — students enjoy the twist when the king's mischief becomes the farmer's relief. Encourage lively voices for the king and farmer characters during read-aloud to help students feel the warm, playful tone.

periods.activity_title: Thinking Through the Story — Comprehension Discussion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.82): five questions on the narrative, discussed orally then written.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the story of the farmer and the king by asking students to name the fruits mentioned and retell what the king did with the grapes. This re-anchors the narrative before the discussion begins.

Let us think — A (p.82): Teacher works through each of the five comprehension questions orally with the class, inviting different students to answer. After discussion, students write their answers in their notebooks.
Teacher reviews answers together as a class, clarifying why the farmer chose grapes over watermelons and what made his 'Thank God!' reply wise and humorous.
Wrap-up: students share in one sentence what they liked most about the farmer's response to the king, reinforcing the theme of wisdom in hindsight.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may conflate the wife's role with the farmer's decision — ensure they see that the wife pointed out the best fruits but the farmer made the choice of grapes for the journey. The phrase 'Thank God!' carries the story's central idea: finding the silver lining, so give it unhurried discussion.

periods.activity_title: Think and Say — Farmers, Crops, and Conversations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.82): three guided oral prompts about farmers and farming.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the conversation by reminding students that the farmer in the story grew fruits. Ask: what else can a farmer grow? Students call out answers freely to warm up.

Let us think — B (p.82): Teacher guides discussion through all three prompts — crops farmers grow, women farmers, and what students would say to a farmer they met. Students respond in turns, building on each other's ideas.
Pair work: students practise what they would say if they met a farmer, taking turns as the student and the farmer in a brief guided exchange. Teacher circulates and prompts shy speakers.
Whole-class share-out: two or three pairs share their exchange. Teacher draws out the idea that farmers do important work and deserve respectful, warm conversation.

periods.teacher_notes: Some students may not be aware of women farmers — this prompt is a good opportunity to expand awareness gently without turning the conversation into a lecture. Accept responses about vegetable farming, paddy, or flower cultivation as valid, drawing from what students know from home or their surroundings.

periods.activity_title: Listening to 'Aachoo!' and Speaking About the Big Elephant

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.85): teacher reads 'Aachoo!' poem aloud; students listen and respond.
Let us speak (p.86): oral prompt — food items to bring a sick elephant.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the listening task: 'I am going to read a poem aloud. Listen carefully — a very big animal has a cold.' Students settle and prepare to listen.

Let us listen (p.85): Teacher reads the 'Aachoo!' poem aloud with expression, giving a clear 'AACHOO!' for the elephant's sneeze. The poem is read three to four times so students can absorb the story and the sound-pattern.
Students respond orally: what did the elephant want to buy? Why couldn't the shop give it a handkerchief? What did the elephant ask for instead? Teacher draws out the humour of size mismatch.

Let us speak (p.86): Teacher directs students to the picture of the sick elephant and the fruit basket. Students take turns saying aloud which food items they would bring to visit the Big Elephant who has a cold, giving a brief reason for each choice.
Quick reflection: teacher asks students which item they heard most often and why they think fruits are a good choice when someone is unwell, connecting back to the story's fruit theme.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'Aachoo!' poem echoes the chapter's warm, humorous tone — the elephant's sneeze and the salesperson's surprise delight students of this age. The speaking task links back to the fruit theme of 'Thank God!': a farmer who grows fruits connects naturally to the question of what food to bring a sick friend.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.86): order the steps of Chandu's fruit salad recipe and write them out.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea of a recipe: steps must go in the right order or the dish won't work. Ask students: when you make something at home, does the order matter? Take a few quick oral responses.

Teacher reads all seven fruit salad steps aloud from p.86 in a jumbled order and asks the class: which step should come first? Guide students to identify the opening step together (Mother cuts some fruits for me) before they work individually.

Let us write (p.86): students work through the activity, numbering and then writing the steps in the correct order in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck by asking 'can you squeeze lemon before you have the fruits ready?'
Class review: teacher invites one student to read their ordered sequence aloud, and the class checks each step together. Correct order is confirmed, and students amend if needed.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often place the 'Finally' step correctly but struggle with the middle sequence — particularly where papaya, apple, and grapes go relative to each other. Encourage them to use the signal words (First, Next, Then, After that, Finally) as ordering clues rather than guessing from content alone.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.83): write opposites of underlined words; heavy/light from the story as anchor.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reminds students that in the story the farmer said watermelons were too heavy for the journey and grapes were light. Write 'heavy' and 'light' on the board as an opposite pair and ask students to name any other opposites they know — a quick paired exchange.

Teacher introduces Let us learn — A (p.83) by reading the first pair aloud: 'thick book — ___ book.' Ask students to predict the opposite from context. Work through one or two examples together before students attempt the remaining pairs independently.
Students complete the four opposite pairs in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and checks, particularly for 'soft/hard' and 'slow/fast' where students may confuse the target word's form.
Class review: teacher reads each item and students call out the answer. Each correct opposite is written on the board so students can self-check and correct their own work.

periods.teacher_notes: The opposite pairs are anchored in the story's own language — heavy/light is the farmer's reasoning — so contextual prediction works well here rather than rote recall. Watch for students writing 'thin' for the thick-book pair but 'small' for the long-journey pair, which signals that they are thinking of general size rather than the specific dimension named.

periods.activity_title: Is and Are — Singular and Plural in Sentences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — B and C (p.84): is/are grammar-in-context; fill in eight sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes two sentences on the board drawn from the story context: 'The grape is sweet.' and 'The grapes are sweet.' Ask students what changed between the two sentences and guide them to notice singular/plural and is/are.

Let us learn — B (p.84): Teacher reads the model sentences aloud and briefly explains the rule — one thing uses 'is', more than one uses 'are'. Students repeat example sentences chorally, substituting different nouns from the classroom.

Let us learn — C (p.84): students complete the eight fill-in-the-blank sentences independently in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and nudges students who pause by asking 'how many things are we talking about here?'

Class review: teacher reads each blank-sentence aloud and students hold up one finger for 'is' or two fingers for 'are' before the answer is confirmed. Disagreements are resolved by returning to the noun in the sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with the farmer's choice between 'the grape' and 'the watermelons', students have intuitive exposure to singular and plural nouns already in this chapter. The finger-signal review keeps the whole class actively responding and exposes hesitation quickly so the teacher can address it on the spot.

periods.activity_title: Fruit Word Hunt — Word Search Grid

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore — A (p.87): find and circle eight fruit words in the word search grid.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to recall all the fruits mentioned across the chapter — grapes, watermelons, papaya, banana, apple, mango, guava, and more. Students call them out as the teacher lists them on the board.

Teacher explains how a word search grid works, demonstrating with one example by tracing a word horizontally on a large version drawn on the board. Students are told to look for words running left-to-right or top-to-bottom in the 8×8 grid on p.87.

Let us explore — A (p.87): students work individually to find and circle all eight fruit words — MANGO, PAPAYA, GRAPES, BANANA, GUAVA, PLUM, PEACH, PEAR — in the grid. Teacher circulates, encouraging students who finish early to help a partner without revealing positions.
Class check: teacher calls out each fruit word one by one and students raise their hand when they have found it. The grid is reviewed together and any missing words are located as a group.

periods.teacher_notes: PAPAYA and BANANA are the longest words in the grid and tend to trip students up — encourage them to look for the first letter confidently and then trace the rest. This word hunt reinforces the fruit vocabulary that runs through the chapter and gives students an enjoyable, low-stakes encounter with word recognition.

periods.activity_title: Bringing It All Together — Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to retell the story of the farmer and the king in three to four sentences, drawing on the narrative of the fruit gift, the grape-throwing, and the farmer's famous reply. Two or three students retell aloud while the class listens and adds any missing detail.

Quick oral round: teacher poses three rapid-fire questions drawing on the chapter's ideas — one about the farmer's choice between grapes and watermelons, one using an opposite-word pair from the chapter's vocabulary, and one asking whether a sentence takes 'is' or 'are'. Students respond by raising hands.

Students write three to four sentences in their notebooks on the prompt: 'If you could give a gift to someone special, what would you choose and why?' They use at least one opposite-word pair and the correct form of 'is' or 'are' in their response. Teacher circulates and offers brief verbal feedback.

Students draw and label three fruits from the chapter on a small box in their notebook, writing one sentence about each using 'is' or 'are' correctly — for example, 'Grapes are small and sweet.' This connects word-work learning to the chapter's fruit theme.

Closing reflection: teacher asks 'When something goes wrong, can we find a reason to say Thank God? Why?' One or two students share briefly. Teacher ends by affirming the story's message of wisdom, gratitude, and finding the silver lining.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the narrative wisdom of the farmer, the vocabulary of opposites, the grammar of is/are, and the fruit language that runs through the chapter. The writing prompt invites personal application of the story's theme — accept any sincere response, not only fruit-related gifts.

items.source_context: Farmer chooses grapes over watermelons as a gift; king throws grapes; farmer says 'Thank God!' with wise reasoning.
items.item_stem: Why did the farmer choose to bring grapes to the king instead of watermelons?

options.label: A
options.text: Grapes were the only fruit the farmer had grown that year.

options.label: B
options.text: His wife told him the king did not like watermelons.

options.label: C
options.text: The king had asked specifically for grapes.

options.label: D
options.text: Watermelons were too heavy to carry on the long journey to the palace.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have missed that the king made no request; the farmer chose freely.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not grasped that the farmer grew several fruits including watermelons and grapes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may be confusing the wife's role — she pointed out the finest fruits, not the king's preference.

items.source_lo: Student infers character motivation and identifies key events using a humorous narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Farmer chooses grapes over watermelons as a gift; king throws grapes; farmer says 'Thank God!' with wise reasoning.
items.item_stem: When the king threw grapes at the farmer one by one, the farmer said 'Thank God!' every time. What was the farmer really thinking? Write one to two sentences explaining his reasoning.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The farmer was grateful that he had brought grapes instead of the heavy watermelons. He realised that if the king had thrown watermelons at his forehead, it would have hurt him badly.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short poem, responds orally, and speaks about a real-world scenario using a narrative and a listening poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Guided talk on farming and farmers; listening to the 'Aachoo!' elephant poem; speaking about food for a sick elephant.
items.item_stem: Listen carefully as your teacher reads the poem 'Aachoo!' aloud. Then answer: Why did the elephant ask for a sheet instead of a handkerchief?

options.text: The elephant decided it did not need anything for its cold.
The elephant sneezed so hard that it blew the handkerchiefs away.
The elephant wanted a handkerchief but the shop did not have one in its size.
The salesgirl was surprised because elephants do not usually visit shops.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true — the shop had no handkerchief big enough for the elephant, so it asked for a sheet instead. Statement 2 is false — the elephant still wanted something for its cold. Statement 3 is true — the salesgirl was surprised by the unusual customer. Statement 4 is false — the poem does not say the elephant's sneeze blew the handkerchiefs away.

items.item_stem: Look at the picture of the Big Elephant on Textbook page 86. The elephant has a cold and you are going to visit it. Say aloud three food items you would bring and give one reason for your choice.

expected_elements: Names at least three specific food items clearly.
Gives a reason connected to health or care.

items.source_lo: Student sequences steps in a logical order and writes them accurately using a procedural writing task as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Ordering seven jumbled steps of Chandu's fruit salad recipe using sequence signal words.
items.item_stem:
Read the two steps below from Chandu's fruit salad. Which one comes first? Write the number 1 or 2 in the box next to each step.

[ ] Finally, I squeeze a lemon on it, adding a pinch of salt.
[ ] First I take some banana slices.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The step 'First I take some banana slices' comes first (number 1). 'Finally, I squeeze a lemon on it, adding a pinch of salt' comes second (number 2), as 'Finally' signals the last step.

items.source_context: Ordering seven jumbled steps of Chandu's fruit salad recipe using sequence signal words.
items.item_stem: Think of something simple you do at home — washing your hands, making a glass of juice, or tidying your bag. Write three to four steps in the correct order. Begin with 'First' and end with 'Finally'.

expected_elements: Steps are in a logical, workable sequence.
Uses at least two sequence signal words.
Each step is written as a clear sentence.
